Seminar Title:

Borrowing Spatial and Climate Information in Risk Modeling for Crop Insurance Pricing

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

School of Management

Speaker Name:

Bhaktideepa Sahu ( Rollno : 522sm2003)

Speaker Type:

Conference Hall (SM302)

22 Sep 2026 16:00

Dushyant Ashok Mahadik

Abstract:

Agricultural production faces increasing exposure to climatic variability, extreme weather, and spatially correlated shocks, creating substantial uncertainty in yield risk. Reliable risk characterization is therefore essential for actuarially sound crop insurance pricing. This research, undertaken in four sequential components, integrates climatic, vegetation, spatial, and distributional dependence within a data-driven method to improve crop-yield risk modelling, enhance premium accuracy, and support efficient agricultural risk transfer.

The first component of this study focuses on the univariate characterization of crop-yield risk, examining uncertainty in the statistical representation of yield distributions using historical yield data from 57 major rice-producing districts across five states. A range of parametric, non-parametric, semi-parametric, and model-averaging approaches are evaluated using both in-sample and out-of-sample predictive criteria. The results demonstrate that the choice of yield-distributional specification materially affects the estimated insurance premiums. Bayesian model averaging provides a more robust representation by accounting for uncertainty arising from alternative model specifications and spatial heterogeneity. Building on this univariate characterization, the second component extends the analysis to a multivariate approach for crop-yield estimation, incorporating information beyond historical yield outcomes. Using district-level data from 67 districts across 10 Indian states, the analysis regresses meteorological and remotely sensed vegetation indicators corresponding to different stages of the crop growth cycle within a district fixed-effects framework. The results show pronounced stage-specific yield responses. The model demonstrates satisfactory predictive performance and highlights the essential agricultural factors to improve crop-yield assessment.

The third component of this dissertation work extends the analysis beyond mean regression to the joint dependence between crop yields and climatic covariates, with particular emphasis on dependence in the tails of their joint distribution. Five copula specifications are examined to capture non-linear dependence structures beyond conventional linear correlations and to assess whether extreme outcomes are jointly realized. The Gaussian and t-copulas provide the best fit for the selected yield&ndashweather relationships, with the latter offering greater flexibility in representing tail dependence. A non-parametric Bayesian framework subsequently incorporates this joint dependence information to construct climate-responsive posterior yield distributions and evaluate adverse climate scenarios. This tail-sensitive characterization provides a more appropriate basis for evaluating extreme yield losses and their implications for climate-responsive insurance premiums. Lastly, the fourth component focuses on the spatial dependence of agricultural risk, which was examined using 452 U.S. counties, where spatially consistent crop-yield and environmental information permit explicit modeling of geographic dependence. Bayesian spatial quantile modeling was used to capture spatial heterogeneity in the conditional yield distribution, while alternative spatial priors and smoothing structures were evaluated for their effects on predictive densities, premium rates, and retain&ndashcede outcomes.

Overall, the findings demonstrate that integrating essential agricultural variables in flexible yield distributions, nonlinear climate dependence, and spatial structure can substantially improve the characterization of production risk and support more accurate, stable, spatially differentiated, and climate-responsive crop insurance pricing and risk transfer.&nbsp

Keywords: Crop Insurance, Risk Modelling, Crop Yield Distribution, Actuarial Fair Premium rate, Remote Sensing Indicators, Bayesian Approach, Copula, Spatial Dependence, Spatial Smoothing, Rating Game, Market Incompleteness
